1345.title: Savitri
1345.hook: a banyan trunk wound with thread: how Savitri is remembered, and how differently she is read
1345.howItsDone: On Vat Savitri, some married Hindu women fast, worship at a banyan tree, wind thread around its trunk and hear Savitri's story told, asking for long lives for their husbands; the day and customs differ by region.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Savitri on the road behind Death, speaking about the good until he stopped to listen.

A banyan tree, its trunk wound round and round with thread. On a festival day called Vat Savitri, some married Hindu women fast, walk around a banyan and tie thread to it, asking for long lives for their husbands. Vat is the banyan. Savitri is the woman from the forest. The tree doesn't come from the epic's telling; it comes from the way the story has been lived since. On our last day with her: how a story becomes a practice, and how one woman can be read more than one way.
screen: `A BANYAN WOUND WITH THREAD.` → `A FESTIVAL IN HER NAME.` → `ONE WOMAN, MORE THAN ONE READING.`

segments.voice: Start with where the epic puts her. The story sits in the Mahabharata's forest book, in a section whose title can be translated as the greatness of the devoted wife. The sage Markandeya tells it because Yudhishthira has asked: has there ever been a woman as devoted as Draupadi? Markandeya's answer is Savitri, and his last word is that Draupadi, like Savitri, will save them all. So the frame is devotion, and some readers keep it. They hear a wife whose faithfulness is strong enough to stop Death, and the vow at the banyan grows out of that reading. Other readers notice different things in the same lines. Her father sends her out to choose her own husband, and she does. Told the man will die, she refuses to choose again. She keeps a hard truth alone for a year. She argues with Death, on the road, as a friend. They hear a woman of fierce will and a sharp mind. And a modern poet, Aurobindo, read her as something else again: the divine word come down to free the soul from death. These readings don't have to cancel each other. Devotion and will can live in one person. What they share is a woman who doesn't sit still when the worst news arrives. She acts. And look at how it ended in the epic: Savitri in the clearing at night, her husband's head in her lap, then picking up his axe and walking him home through the dark.
screen: `THE GREATNESS OF THE DEVOTED WIFE` · `SOME READ DEVOTION STRONG AS DEATH` · `SOME READ A WILL AND A SHARP MIND` · `SHE ACTS WHEN THE WORST NEWS COMES`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose life you'd ask to be long, and hold their face for a moment. Then, slowly, as if winding thread around a tree, go round them in your mind, their morning, their work, their evening, their sleep, one slow circle for each breath. If you pray, you can pray for them.
Savitri. Told as the greatness of a devoted wife, read by others as a woman of will, and remembered at a banyan wound with thread.
Your line: Savitri. One story, and more than one way to love it. Rest well.

1346.title: Damayanti
1346.hook: five men stand in the hall with one face, and Damayanti chooses the one with dust on him
1346.howItsDone: Hindus hear Damayanti's story in the Mahabharata's forest book, where the sage Brihadashva tells it to Yudhishthira; it is also retold in later poems, plays and dance across India.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Savitri at the banyan, read as devotion, as will and as the divine word. Today, a new woman, and a hall full of gods.
screen: `SHE ACTS WHEN THE WORST NEWS COMES.`

segments.voice: Five men in a row, every one with the same face. That's what Damayanti sees when she walks into her own swayamvara, garland in hand, ready to choose. Four of them are gods wearing the face of the man she loves. One of them is the man. Last year we heard the whole story of Nala and Damayanti, from a golden swan to a long reunion. This time we stay with her: three days, three choices, and the first is made in a hall full of gods.
screen: `FIVE MEN, ONE FACE.` → `FOUR GODS AND A MAN.` → `HER FIRST CHOICE.`

segments.voice: Damayanti is the daughter of King Bhima of Vidarbha. She has chosen Nala in her heart before she ever sees him, because a swan carried his praises to her. Then the gods want her too: Indra, Agni, Varuna and Yama. They make Nala, of all people, carry their offer. She tells him plainly: she is his, and she'll choose him in front of the gods so no blame falls on him. On the day, the gods come as Nala. She can't tell them apart, so she doesn't guess. In her heart she bows to the gods and asks them, by the truth of her promise, to show themselves. And they do. The gods don't sweat. Their eyes don't blink. Their garlands stay fresh, there's no dust on them, their feet don't quite touch the ground, and they cast no shadow. One figure has a shadow, sweat on his skin, dust on him, a garland starting to wilt, and eyes that blink. That's the one she garlands. On one side, gods: perfect, unfading, without a speck on them. On the other, a man who gets dusty and tired, whose flowers die. Every sign that gives him away is a sign of being mortal, and that's exactly how she finds him. She doesn't love him in spite of the dust. The dust is how she knows him. And the gods aren't angry. The story says they bless the couple and give Nala gifts. Perfection, here, steps aside for a person who blinks.
screen: `SHE CHOSE HIM BEFORE SHE SAW HIM` · `SHE ASKS THE GODS BY HER PROMISE` · `NO SWEAT, NO BLINK, NO SHADOW` · `SHE GARLANDS THE ONE WITH DUST`

1347.title: Damayanti
1347.hook: a husband has vanished, and Damayanti sends out not soldiers but a question
1347.howItsDone: Hindus know Damayanti's search from the Mahabharata's forest book, where Brihadashva tells it to the exiled Yudhishthira; it is also retold in later poems, plays and dance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Damayanti in the hall of five faces, choosing the one with dust and a shadow.

How do you find someone who doesn't want to be found? Damayanti's husband lost everything at dice, walked into the forest with her, cut their one shared cloth while she slept, and left. She survived the forest and made her way home to her father's house in Vidarbha, to her children. Nala is out there somewhere, changed, hidden, ashamed. A king's daughter could send riders. Damayanti sends something smaller and sharper. Her second choice: how to search.
screen: `HE DOESN'T WANT TO BE FOUND.` → `HOME IN VIDARBHA.` → `HER SECOND CHOICE.`

segments.voice: She calls Brahmanas, travelers who go from court to court, and gives them a question to repeat wherever people gather. In paraphrase: where have you gone, gambler, after cutting half the cloth of the wife who loved you and leaving her asleep in the forest? She's still waiting, wearing half a cloth. Have mercy, and answer. Don't say who sent you, she adds. If anyone answers, notice who he is and where he lives, and bring me his words. Look at how the question is built. It isn't an accusation shouted in a square. It names only things two people would know: a gambler, a cut cloth, a sleeping wife. A stranger hears a riddle. The one man it's meant for hears his own story. And it asks him to answer, which leaves him room to speak instead of run. Then a messenger, in a far city, reports back. A plain charioteer heard the words and answered with a strange defense of a husband who had even lost his cloth to the birds. Nobody but Nala would know that detail. Damayanti doesn't rush. She tells her mother and asks that her father not be told yet. Then she sets a careful trap: word goes out that she'll choose a husband again, tomorrow, so soon that only a driver with Nala's skill could bring a king there in time. When the chariot arrives, she sends her maid Keshini to watch the charioteer. Then she sends their children to him, and she watches him weep. Only then does she let him in. She doesn't trust rumor. She tests with love.
screen: `ONE QUESTION, CARRIED FAR` · `ONLY HE WOULD KNOW THE ANSWER` · `A CHARIOTEER ANSWERS` · `SHE TESTS BEFORE SHE TRUSTS`

1348.title: Damayanti
1348.hook: the man who left her asks why she would choose again, and Damayanti has to answer
1348.howItsDone: Hindus know Nala and Damayanti's reunion from the Mahabharata's forest book; the sage tells it to Yudhishthira, who had also lost his kingdom at dice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Damayanti's search: one question carried from court to court, and a test before she trusted.

Nala and Damayanti are face to face at last, in her father's house, after the forest, the cut cloth, the long separation. He still wears the changed, unlovely shape that has hidden him. And the first hard thing out of his mouth is a question for her: how could a faithful wife send out word that she'd choose another husband? The man who walked away is asking her to account for herself. Her third choice: what to say to that.
screen: `FACE TO FACE AT LAST.` → `HE ASKS THE HARD QUESTION.` → `HER THIRD CHOICE.`

segments.voice: First, what she does before he asks. When she sees him, the story says, she speaks with grief and no softening: what kind of man leaves a sleeping wife alone in the forest? Who would do that, except Nala? She says it to his face. And Nala doesn't defend himself as a man who was right. He tells her it wasn't fully him: Kali, the spirit of strife, had entered him, and was in him when he lost the kingdom and when he left her. Now Kali is gone. Then he asks his question about the second swayamvara, and Damayanti answers it straight. It was never real, she says. It was a way to bring him to Vidarbha, because only he could drive a king there in a single day. She swears to her faithfulness. Then the story brings a witness: a voice from the sky, the wind itself speaking, says she has kept faith with him the whole time. Look at the shape of the scene. Each of them has to be believed. He, that the man who left her was not all of him. She, that the swayamvara was a trap made of love. Neither skips the hard part. She names the wound. He names what drove him. The truth is spoken out loud, and only then does he put on the serpent's garment and become himself again. They hold each other, and the story says they talk until morning, telling each other what happened in the forest. That's how this marriage is mended: with words, both ways.
screen: `SHE NAMES THE WOUND` · `HE NAMES WHAT DROVE HIM` · `THE WIND SAYS SHE KEPT FAITH` · `MENDED WITH WORDS, BOTH WAYS`

If you pray, you can pray for that mending.

1349.title: Shakuntala
1349.hook: a baby left by a river in the forest, and birds standing guard around her
1349.howItsDone: Hindus know Shakuntala's story from the Mahabharata's first book, the Adi Parva, and from the poet Kalidasa's later play about her; her birth is told in both.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Damayanti and Nala face to face, mending a marriage with words both ways. Today, a new woman, before her story begins.

A newborn lies alone on a riverbank in the forest. No mother nearby. No village. And around her, keeping off whatever might come out of the trees, are birds. That's how the Mahabharata's first book begins the life of Shakuntala, a stranger start than the love story people remember. A king will come. Today we stay before he arrives, with a girl, the birds, and the old hermit who heard her cry.
screen: `A NEWBORN ON A RIVERBANK.` → `BIRDS STANDING GUARD.` → `BEFORE THE KING ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: In the epic, Shakuntala tells her own beginning to a visitor, the way she heard it from the sage Kanva, who raised her. It starts with another sage, Vishvamitra, whose austerities are so fierce that Indra, king of the gods, grows afraid of his power. Indra sends the apsara Menaka, a celestial dancer, to break his concentration. She does. A daughter is born. Menaka leaves the baby beside a river in the forest and goes back to heaven. So the girl's parents are a great sage and a heavenly woman, and neither stays. Then the birds gather around the baby and protect her in that lonely place. Kanva, out for his bath, finds her, brings her home to his hermitage and raises her as his daughter. He names her for the birds. The epic's word for bird is shakunta, so she is Shakuntala, the one the birds protected. That's the epic's own explanation of her name. Kanva also lists who counts as a father: the one who gives life, the one who saves a life, and the one who gives food. By that measure, he is fully her father. That changes the romance ahead. Before she is anyone's beloved, Shakuntala is a child who was left, and then kept. Her name doesn't remember her famous parents. It remembers the small creatures who stood guard, and the old man who chose her. Whatever comes later starts here, with a girl who knows exactly who took care of her.
screen: `VISHVAMITRA, MENAKA, AND A DAUGHTER` · `LEFT BY THE RIVER, GUARDED BY BIRDS` · `KANVA NAMES HER FOR THE BIRDS` · `LIFE, SAFETY AND FOOD MAKE A FATHER`

1350.title: Shakuntala
1350.hook: a king calls out at an empty hermitage, and the woman who answers sets terms before she says yes
1350.howItsDone: Hindus know this part of Shakuntala's story from the Mahabharata's first book, the Adi Parva, where the meeting and the gandharva marriage take place at Kanva's hermitage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shakuntala as a newborn by the river, guarded by birds and named for them by Kanva.

Who is here? That's the first thing King Dushyanta says at the hermitage. He has been hunting, has left his soldiers behind, and walks into the quiet place where the sage Kanva lives and calls out. Kanva isn't home. A young woman comes out instead, dressed like an ascetic, and welcomes him the way a host should. Then the king proposes marriage, almost at once, and the story waits to see what she'll say. What she says is not quite yes.
screen: `WHO IS HERE?` → `THE SAGE IS AWAY.` → `NOT QUITE YES.`

segments.voice: First, the welcome. Shakuntala offers the king a seat and water and asks after his health, the duties of a host, and tells him her father has gone to gather fruit. Wait, she says; he'll be back soon. The king asks who she is, and she tells him her birth: the sage, the apsara, the birds. Then he asks her to marry him. Her first answer is patience. Wait for my father, she says. He will give me to you. The king answers with law. There is a form of marriage called the gandharva, he says, made by two people's own choice, and it's lawful for a king. She can give herself. And here Shakuntala does the thing the rest of her story hangs on. She agrees, on one condition: promise that the son born of me will be your heir and rule after you. Only if you promise this. The king promises. They marry. He leaves for his city, saying he'll send a proper escort to bring her to the palace. Then Kanva comes home. The epic says he knows what happened through his own inner sight, and he isn't angry. He's glad, blesses her, and tells her the marriage is a good one. Time goes by. She gives birth to a son, who grows up in the hermitage so strong he tames the wild animals of the forest; the hermits call him the all-tamer. And from the city, nobody comes. Hold on to the condition she set. Young, alone, asked by a king, she didn't just say yes. She asked for a promise, out loud. Tomorrow, she carries that promise into court.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shakuntala at the hermitage, saying yes to a king only on a promise spoken aloud.

A crowded royal hall, and a woman holding a boy by the hand. No one ever came from the city, so Kanva has sent Shakuntala and her son to the king. She bows and says it plainly: this is your son. Make him your heir, as you promised me at the hermitage. King Dushyanta looks at her and says he doesn't know her, never married her, has no idea who she is. Everyone is watching. segments.voice: For a moment, the epic says, she can't move. She stands there stunned, ashamed and furious at once, her eyes going red. Then she speaks, for a long time. Here is some of it, in paraphrase. First, witnesses. You think you're alone with what you did, she tells him, but the sun and the moon, the wind and fire, the earth and the sky, your own heart, all of them saw. You know, and you're saying you don't. Second, the boy. A son is his father born again; look at him and you see yourself, as if in a mirror. Third, when the king answers with insults about her mother the apsara and her birth in the forest, she turns his words around. You can see other people's faults when they're as small as a mustard seed, she says, and you can't see your own when they're as big as a bilva fruit. She never begs. She never pretends the promise was smaller than it was. She stands in a king's own hall and tells him the truth about himself. When he still refuses, she turns to go. Then a voice from the sky tells the king that she speaks the truth, and that the boy is his son. Only then does Dushyanta take them in. This is a week's end, so look back. The week began with Savitri remembered at a banyan. Then Damayanti, choosing the mortal, searching with a question, naming the wound. And now Shakuntala, in a hall full of people, refusing to be unknown.
